QUESTION 1 OF 6
Can strangers trust each other without a middleman?
Every payment you make today relies on someone in the middle. In 2008, someone found another way.
Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
QUESTION 1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
The internet started open, then centralized
WEB 1 · 1980s–2000s
Open protocols
TCP/IP, HTTP, email. Nobody owns them, and anyone can build on them without asking permission.
WEB 2 · 2000s–NOW
Closed platforms
A few companies hold the users, the data and the rules. They attract you first, then extract from you.
WEB 3 · THE BET
Open networks that hold value
Networks owned by their users, with rules enforced by code that everyone can read.
Chris Dixon (a16z): software networks, unlike phone or TV networks, can be re-architected, and blockchains are that re-architecture.
Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
Reading: Chris Dixon, "Why Decentralization Matters" (2018)
The hard problem: digital money can be copied
A digital coin is just data, and data can be copied. What stops Alice from paying the same coin twice?
Alice
owns coin #42
Bob
receives coin #42
Carol
also receives coin #42
same coin, twice
Who really got paid?
The old fix: a trusted middleman
A bank keeps the one true ledger and rejects the second payment. It works, but now the bank is the hub.
Bitcoin's fix: everyone keeps the ledger
Thousands of computers hold a copy and agree on the order of payments. The first spend wins; the second is rejected.
Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
THE BREAKTHROUGH, 2008
2008: Bitcoin, money without a bank
On 31 October 2008, in the middle of a global banking crisis, someone calling themselves Satoshi Nakamoto posted a nine-page paper to a cryptography mailing list.
It answered the double-spend problem without any trusted party: a shared ledger, copied on every node, extended block by block.
The first block, mined in January 2009, carries a newspaper headline: "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks."
What Bitcoin proved
  • Digital scarcity is possible
  • Strangers can agree without identities
  • Incentives can secure a network
  • Code can hold real value

A hash is a fingerprint
Feed any data into a hash function and you get a short fingerprint. Change one character and the fingerprint changes completely.
So tampering is loud
Edit one payment in block 101 and its fingerprint changes, so block 102 no longer matches, and nor does any block after it.

Live: this laptop is mining right now
A real SHA-256 race at a toy difficulty of three zeros. Real Bitcoin blocks need around nineteen.
Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
What removing the middleman buys, and costs
No permission needed
Anyone can run a node, send a payment or launch an app. There is no gatekeeper to apply to.
No single point of failure
Thousands of independent machines agree on one history. Switch one off and nothing happens.
Rules you can read
The rules are open code, and changing them needs public agreement, not a board meeting.
The price
Everything is public, nothing can be quietly undone, and there is no customer support. Remember this card in question 5.
Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
A revolution with a tiny instruction set
Bitcoin's scripting language is deliberately limited: no loops and almost no memory. Perfect for one job, moving coins safely, and nearly useless for anything else.
By 2013, developers wanted lending, exchanges, voting and games, and each idea needed its own new blockchain built from scratch.
A 19-year-old asked: why not one chain that can run any program?
BITCOIN
A calculator: one job, done provably, forever
ETHEREUM
A computer: runs any program you can pay for
Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
2015: Ethereum, the world computer
The EVM
One shared virtual machine. Every node runs the same code and reaches the same result; that agreement is the product.
Two kinds of accounts
People, controlled by private keys, and contracts, controlled by code. Both can hold money and act.
Gas
Every instruction has a price paid in ETH. You pay for what you compute, so an endless loop simply runs out of money.
2013
Whitepaper
2014
Public crowdsale
JUL 2015
Launch ("Frontier"), on Proof of Work
Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
Reading: ethereum.org/whitepaper
Smart contracts: vending machines for agreements
Insert a coin, get a snack, no shopkeeper needed. A smart contract applies that idea to any agreement: escrow, auctions, loans, insurance, certificates.
  • Deployed once: nobody, not even its author, can quietly change it
  • Runs exactly as written: a promise, and a threat
  • Holds its own money: a bug is not a crash, it is an open vault
Escrow.sol · Solidity
contract Escrow {   address buyer;   address seller;   function release() external {     require(msg.sender == buyer);     payable(seller).transfer(       address(this).balance);   } }

Ownership receipts for digital things: art, game items, tickets, certificates.

Q1 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
What happens when you press "Send"
01
Sign
Your wallet signs it with your private key
02
Broadcast
It waits in a public queue, the mempool
03
Order
A block builder picks it and sets its place
04
Propose
A validator adds the block to the chain
05
Execute
Every node runs it on the EVM and updates state
06
Finalize
After ~13 minutes it can never be undone
STEP 02 IS PUBLIC
Bots can see your trade before it lands, and jump ahead of it.
STEP 03 IS POWER
Whoever orders transactions decides who gets in, and in what order.
STEP 06 IS SLOW
Thirteen minutes to "final" is an eternity for payments.

Q2 · CHANGING THE ENGINE MID-FLIGHT
THE NEW ENGINE
From burning electricity to putting money at risk
Proof of Work
Proof of Stake
Who writes blocks
Miners with specialised hardware
Validators who lock up 32 ETH
Security comes from
Electricity spent on guessing
Money posted as collateral
If you cheat
You wasted your electricity
Your stake is destroyed ("slashed")
Energy use
Very high
~99.95% lower
New ETH issued
High, to pay for mining
About 90% lower
The intuition: instead of proving you burned resources, you prove you have something to lose.
Q2 · CHANGING THE ENGINE MID-FLIGHT
Figures: ethereum.org, The Merge
How Proof of Stake picks who writes the next block
01 · STAKE
Deposit 32 ETH to become a validator. The deposit is your bond.
02 · PROPOSE
Every 12-second slot, one validator is picked at random to propose a block.
03 · ATTEST
Committees of other validators vote that the block is valid.
04 · FINALIZE
Once two-thirds of all stake has voted over two epochs (~13 min), the block is final.
1 EPOCH = 32 SLOTS × 12 SECONDS = 6.4 MINUTES · one proposer per slot
Slashing
Sign two conflicting blocks or votes and part of your stake is destroyed, and you are thrown out.
Why final means final
Reverting a finalized block would need at least a third of all staked ETH to be slashed: billions destroyed on purpose.

Q2 · CHANGING THE ENGINE MID-FLIGHT
The Merge: swapping the engine in mid-flight
EXECUTION CHAIN · PROOF OF WORK · SINCE 2015
BEACON CHAIN · PROOF OF STAKE · SINCE 2020
15 SEP 2022 · THE MERGE
ETHEREUM TODAY: ONE CHAIN, TWO LAYERS
ethereum.org's analogy: Ethereum was a spaceship already in flight. Engineers built a new engine alongside it, tested it for nearly two years, then swapped it in without stopping the ship.
On the day, users noticed nothing. Every account, balance and contract carried over; the old chain kept running transactions, and the Beacon Chain took over deciding who adds blocks.

QUESTION 3 OF 6
Who decides what goes into a block, and how fast?
Ordering transactions is power, and power is worth money. Ethereum's own roadmap is still working on it.
Q3 · WHO DECIDES, AND HOW FAST
Ethereum's own to-do list
In 2026 the Ethereum Foundation published the Strawmap, an open draft plan to 2030. Its five goals are five unsolved problems:
Fast L1
Finality in seconds
Today: a block every 12 seconds, final after about 13 minutes.
Gigagas L1
~10,000 TPS on L1
1 billion gas per second, via zkEVMs and real-time proving.
Teragas L2
~10M TPS on L2s
1 gigabyte per second of rollup data, via data availability sampling.
Post-quantum L1
Safe for centuries
Cryptography that quantum computers cannot break, via hash-based schemes.
Private L1
Privacy by default
Privacy as a first-class citizen, via shielded transfers.
Up next: speed and fairness. Privacy and quantum safety come in question 4.
The full map: strawmap.org
Q3 · WHO DECIDES, AND HOW FAST
Source: strawmap.org, "five simple north stars"
THE SPEED PROBLEM
Why does "final" take 13 minutes?
Today
~13 min
Strawmap goal
seconds
Why it matters
Exchanges, payments and bridges between chains must wait for finality before they can safely treat money as received.
Why it is hard
Hundreds of thousands of validators must vote. Gathering and combining their signatures in seconds is a networking and cryptography problem.
The catch
Faster blocks favour big, well-connected operators. Speed must not cost decentralization.
Q3 · WHO DECIDES, AND HOW FAST
Sources: strawmap.org · Vitalik Buterin on fast finality (Sep 2026)
THE FAIRNESS PROBLEM
Who decides what gets into a block?
You
submit a token swap
Mempool
public: bots see it first
Builder
orders transactions for maximum profit
Relay
a trusted middleman passes the block on
Proposer
signs the most profitable block
MEV
Profit from ordering. A bot buys just before your trade and sells just after: a "sandwich". A few builders now make most blocks.
ePBS · Glamsterdam
Enshrined proposer-builder separation writes the builder–proposer deal into the protocol, removing the trusted relay.
FOCIL
Inclusion lists let many validators force transactions in, so a handful of builders cannot censor them.

QUESTION 4 OF 6
Can money be private and still be trusted?
Today, every payment on Ethereum is visible to the whole world, forever.
Q4 · PRIVATE AND TRUSTED
THE PRIVACY PROBLEM
Today, every transaction is a postcard
TODAY · POSTCARD
from: 0x3a…91 to: 0x7f…c2 amount: 2.4 ETH · history: all of it
Anyone can read who paid whom, how much, and everything before it, forever.
GOAL · SEALED ENVELOPE
from: ████████ to: ████████ amount: ████ · valid: ✓ proven
A shielded transfer: the network checks it is valid without reading what is inside.
Why it matters
Public balances paint targets: thieves know exactly who holds what.
Being built
Privacy inside ordinary wallets; Privacy Pools prove funds are clean without revealing history.
The stakes
Without privacy, the EF's privacy team warns of "the backbone of global surveillance."
Q4 · PRIVATE AND TRUSTED
Sources: Vitalik, L1 privacy roadmap (Apr 2025) · PSE roadmap (Sep 2025)
The tool behind it all: zero-knowledge proofs
PROVER
Knows a secret: a balance, an identity, a model's weights
PROOF
A few hundred bytes, checkable in milliseconds
VERIFIER
Learns the statement is true, and nothing else
The Where's Waldo trick: cover the page with a big sheet that has one Waldo-sized hole. You prove you found him without revealing where he is on the page.
Privacy
Pay, vote or show a certificate without exposing yourself
Scaling
Prove a whole block was run correctly, so laptops can check it
AI
Prove a model really produced an answer (act 6)
Q4 · PRIVATE AND TRUSTED
Idea: Goldwasser, Micali & Rackoff (1985)
THE QUANTUM PROBLEM
A clock nobody can see
Every wallet and validator is protected by elliptic-curve signatures. A large enough quantum computer could work out private keys from public ones. Nobody knows when, and moving a live network takes years, so the work starts now.
TODAY
Elliptic-curve keys everywhere
STEP 1
Register post-quantum keys
STEP 2
Migrate wallets and validators
GOAL
Hash-based signatures only
The plan
Signatures whose security rests only on hash functions, rolled out over several forks.
The bet
The EF formed a post-quantum team in January 2026, with $1M in prizes for hash-function research.
Still hard
The new signatures are far bigger, and every user must move. What about lost or forgotten wallets?

QUESTION 5 OF 6
What happens when code can't be patched?
A smart contract can't be hot-fixed. When it fails, the money is usually gone.
Q5 · CODE THAT CAN'T BE PATCHED
LIGHTNING ROUND · MYTH OR FACT?
THUMBS UP = FACT · DOWN = MYTH
Four claims. Vote with your thumbs.
CLAIM 1
Bitcoin and Ethereum are anonymous.
MYTH ✗
Bitcoin and Ethereum are anonymous.
Only pseudonymous. Every transaction is public forever; link one address to your name and your whole history is exposed.
CLAIM 2
Send crypto to the wrong address and your bank can reverse it.
MYTH ✗
Send crypto to the wrong address and your bank can reverse it.
There is no bank and no undo button. Always double-check the address before you sign.
CLAIM 3
One bug froze over 500,000 ETH, and it is still stuck.
FACT ✓
One bug froze over 500,000 ETH, and it is still stuck.
Parity wallet, November 2017: a user accidentally broke a shared library and 513,774 ETH was frozen for good.
CLAIM 4
Quantum computers can break Ethereum's keys today.
MYTH ✗
Quantum computers can break Ethereum's keys today.
Not yet. Nobody knows when, so Ethereum is already planning a switch to quantum-safe signatures.

QUICK QUIZ · 4 OF 4
SHOUT YOUR ANSWER
In February 2025, attackers stole $1.5 billion from the exchange Bybit. What did they actually break?
A
Ethereum's cryptography
B

Q5 · CODE THAT CAN'T BE PATCHED
CASE STUDY · KEYS AND SIGNING
Bybit, February 2025: the screen lied
01 BREACH
Attackers break into a developer's machine at the wallet software provider
02 PLANT
They hide malicious code in the web page the signers use
03 DISGUISE
Bybit's signers see what looks like a routine transfer
04 SIGN
They approve it, really handing control of the cold wallet to the attacker
05 DRAIN
About 401,000 ETH, worth ~$1.5B, is moved out
No contract was broken
The multi-signature wallet did exactly what it was told. The humans were shown the wrong thing.
Open problem
What you see must be what you sign: readable, independently verified transaction displays.
Who
The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea's "TraderTraitor" group.
Q5 · CODE THAT CAN'T BE PATCHED
Sources: FBI attribution · post-incident reporting, Feb–Mar 2025
CHALLENGE · FIRST CORRECT ANSWER WINS
30 SECONDS
Spot the bug that could drain this contract
function withdraw() {   uint amount = balance[msg.sender];   require(amount > 0);   msg.sender.call{value: amount}("");   balance[msg.sender] = 0; }
HINT
Look at the order of the last two lines. What if whoever receives the money is itself a contract?
The bug: it sends the money before setting the balance to zero. If the receiver's code calls withdraw() again, the balance is still full, so it gets paid again, and again. This exact pattern drained The DAO in 2016.
Q5 · CODE THAT CAN'T BE PATCHED
The visibility problem: most contracts can't be read
<5%
of roughly 60 million deployed Ethereum contracts have published source code
WHAT DEVS WRITE
function withdraw() { … }
Readable, auditable
WHAT THE CHAIN STORES
0x608060405234 8015600f57…
Bytecode, no names, often obfuscated
Decompile
Turn bytecode back into something a human or a tool can audit.
See through obfuscation
Scammers deliberately scramble code. Can we detect it, or undo it?
Analyse at scale
Millions of contracts, too many for humans. This is where AI comes in.
Q5 · CODE THAT CAN'T BE PATCHED
QUESTION 6 OF 6
What happens when AI holds the money?
AI agents can now hold wallets and pay for things. They can also be tricked, and they can attack.
Q6 · AI HOLDING THE MONEY
THE BIG PICTURE
AI centralizes. Crypto decentralizes.
AI today
  • A few labs control the frontier models and the compute
  • You cannot check which model answered you, or what trained it
  • Fake people and fake content are almost free to make
  • AI agents cannot open bank accounts
What blockchains add
  • Open, permissionless access that no one can revoke
  • Verifiable computation and public, tamper-evident records
  • Proof that a person, or an agent, is unique
  • Money that software can hold and spend
AI is getting more powerful and more concentrated. Blockchains are good at exactly the trust problems that creates.
Q6 · AI HOLDING THE MONEY
Framing: a16z crypto, "AI x crypto: what, where, how"
Agents that find, trust and pay each other
01 NEED
An AI agent needs a dataset to finish its task
02 DISCOVER
Finds providers in the ERC-8004 identity registry
03 CHECK
Reads their reputation, recorded onchain
04 PAY
Server replies "402: Payment Required"; the agent pays cents in stablecoins
05 REVIEW
Gets the data and leaves feedback onchain
ERC-8004
Live on Ethereum since late January 2026: registries for identity, reputation and validation. 49,000+ agents registered by mid-February.
x402
Revives the web's unused HTTP 402 code for pay-per-request. Google has worked with Coinbase on agent payments.
Still open
Fake agents gaming reputation, and agents tricked by prompt injection into signing bad transactions.
Q6 · AI HOLDING THE MONEY
Sources: Cointelegraph (Feb 2026) · Chainstack, ERC-8004 explainer
The twist: AI is already breaking smart contracts
SHARE OF RECENTLY HACKED CONTRACTS AI AGENTS COULD EXPLOIT
A year earlier
2%
Late 2025
55.8%
Simulated exploit revenue on these contracts rose from about $5,000 to $4.6 million, roughly doubling every 1.3 months.
The study
SCONE-bench: 405 contracts really exploited in 2020–2025, attacked in simulation by frontier AI agents.
New bugs, not just old ones
Scanning 2,849 live contracts with no known flaws, agents found two brand-new vulnerabilities.
So defenders need AI too
AI auditors, AI-assisted formal verification, and tools that read the 95% of contracts nobody can.
Q6 · AI HOLDING THE MONEY
Source: Anthropic & MATS, SCONE-bench study (Dec 2025)
Six questions. None fully answered.
01 · TRUST WITHOUT A MIDDLEMAN
Still open: Can networks stay decentralised as they grow, when power keeps pooling in a few hands?
02 · CHANGING THE ENGINE MID-FLIGHT
Still open: How do you keep upgrading a system that nobody owns, without breaking it?
03 · WHO DECIDES, AND HOW FAST
Still open: Can transaction ordering be fair when it is worth money, and can finality take seconds?
04 · PRIVATE AND TRUSTED
Still open: Can payments be private without becoming a haven for crime, and survive quantum computers?
05 · CODE THAT CAN'T BE PATCHED
Still open: How do we audit the 95% of contracts that nobody can read?
06 · AI HOLDING THE MONEY
Still open: How do we stop agents with wallets from being tricked, or turned into attackers?
Pick one. Read about it tonight. Bring your answer to Devcon.
